title: Five lucky winners take home Knicks-themed trash bins like one that cost JP Morgan exec her job - New York Post
content: See more of our coverage in your search results. Five lucky New Yorkers scored some big buckets Friday — when they each took home a Knicks-themed metal trash can, just like the one a JP Morgan executive lost her job for stealing during the team’s NBA Finals victory parade last month. The city’s Sanitation Department plucked the lucky crew from an incredible 125,000 applicants as part of the “No Need to Knick a Bin” contest. “People are getting fired over these!” winner Alfonso Bravo, of Kingsbridge Heights, said after he was awarded the branded trash bin. The winners were unveiled Friday at a celebration at the DSNY’s Upper West Side garage, where each was handed their spoils before a jealous crowd. They were selected at random as part of the contest, which the DSNY launched as a not-so-subtle dig at Angie Baez, who went viral for stealing a painted bin off the Knicks ticker tape parade route last month. The former JP Morgan executive was caught spilling the contents of the basket onto the streets before lugging her new 30-pound prize home via the subway. “We all saw on video that they can be carried away, and I appreciate all of you who are about to do so with our permission,” said DSNY Commissioner Gregory Anderson. “May these baskets remind all New Yorkers that keeping our city clean is always in bounds. Trash belongs in a basket or a bin — not on the sidewalk. Bravo of the Bronx, Daniel LaVert of Brooklyn, Mia Manantan of Manhattan, Gabriela Manzanares, of Queens and Scott Simas, of Staten Island’s Dongan Hills made up the winning team. The five victors each represented one borough — and the DSNY emphasized that the only qualifications the candidates needed to meet were the ability to get the 30-pound baskets out of the Upper West Side office and bring them home. Being a Knicks fan, however, was not a requirement. “I’m more of an interior design fan than a sports fan. I love New York though, so it’s cool to be able to celebrate with everyone and to have this one-of-a-kind piece,” admitted LaVert, originally of Chicago and now living in Bedford-Stuyvesant. “I feel like Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. It’s like my golden ticket!” he continued, saying he would use it for storage. Manathan, of East Harlem, told The Post she thought she was receiving a “scam email” when the DSNY let her know she won. “I’m just happy to have it. Wow, what a one in a million chance of winning!” she said, adding that she now has to figure out where to put it. “It’s a good conversation starter in a traditional New York City apartment. title: JPMorgan cuts Rollins to Neutral on demand uncertainty, slashes price target - Yahoo! Finance Canada
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Investing.com -- JPMorgan downgraded Rollins to Neutral from Overweight and cut its price target to $45 from $70, saying uncertainty around weakening residential demand and a slower-than-expected margin recovery has made the pest control company's near-term risk-reward less compelling despite its intact long-term growth story. The brokerage said questions raised at Rollins' investor day outweighed the answers, particularly around the sharp slowdown in consumer-initiated demand and the timing of a margin recovery. Management said demand patterns had become more volatile than at any point in nearly a decade, while noting customer retention remained strong and suggesting changes in AI-powered search could be affecting lead generation, though the impact remains difficult to quantify. JPMorgan analyst Tomohiko Sano lowered fiscal 2026 and 2027 revenue growth forecasts to 8.7% and 8.4%, respectively, while reducing adjusted EBITDA margin estimates to 21.9% and 22.2%. The brokerage also cut adjusted EPS estimates to $1.17 for 2026 and $1.26 for 2027. The downgrade follows a weaker-than-expected second quarter, with revenue and margins missing expectations as residential brands dependent on search, digital marketing and inbound calls saw declining lead volumes. Residential organic growth slowed to 3.6%, while recurring revenue and relationship-driven businesses such as HomeTeam and Fox remained more resilient. JPMorgan said Rollins entered the peak season with a cost structure built for stronger growth, leading to profitability pressure as demand softened. Management has lowered its 2026 incremental EBITDA margin target to at least 10% from its longer-term framework of 30%-35%, although it expects improvement to be weighted toward the fourth quarter and reaffirmed confidence in its long-term growth algorithm. title: Why is JPMorgan Chase Expanding its Branch Network in a Digital Age - Kavout | AI
content: JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), the largest U.S. bank, is embarking on an ambitious physical expansion, planning to open over 160 new branches across 30+ states in 2026 and aiming for 500 new locations by 2027. This strategy appears to defy the broader industry trend of branch closures, with competitors like Bank of America and Wells Fargo having significantly reduced their physical footprints. The bank's leadership believes that a robust physical presence remains a critical component of its long-term growth, even as digital banking continues its rapid ascent. This move is part of a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar investment to grow and modernize its branch network, including renovating 1,700 existing locations. The goal isn't merely to add more brick-and-mortar; it's a strategic play to deepen customer relationships, enhance cross-selling opportunities, and extend the bank's reach into new and underserved markets. JPMorgan's approach is a calculated bet on a hybrid model, combining its top-ranked digital platform with an accessible physical footprint to capture a wider array of customer needs. The market's initial reaction to this aggressive spending, alongside significant AI investments, was notably negative. Following its Q4 2025 earnings report on January 13, 2026, JPM shares fell 3.8% in a single day, primarily due to an "expense shock" in its 2026 guidance. Management projected expenses to balloon to $105 billion this year, up from $96 billion in 2025. This substantial increase, driven by both AI and physical expansion, signals a period of heavy investment that could weigh on short-term profitability but is designed to fortify the bank's position for the future. Despite the short-term market jitters, JPMorgan's leadership, under CEO Jamie Dimon, has historically used periods of uncertainty to consolidate power and invest for the long haul. The current strategy aligns with this "fortress" mentality, aiming to ensure the bank remains a dominant force, capable of weathering economic shifts and capitalizing on flight-to-quality dynamics during potential market corrections. This expansion is not a retreat from digital, but rather a complementary effort to serve diverse customer segments more effectively. JPMorgan's decision to double down on physical branches is a nuanced strategy, recognizing that while digital channels handle the bulk of routine transactions, human interaction remains crucial for complex financial needs and relationship building. The bank's data indicates that branches are highly effective in driving growth, reporting a 30% increase in consumer and small business customers between 2019 and 2022, and an impressive $85 billion in deposit growth from branches since 2017. This suggests that physical locations are not obsolete but are evolving into advisory hubs. The bank is employing a highly segmented strategy, tailoring branch designs and services to specific customer types. For instance, J.P. Morgan Financial Centers offer concierge-style service for affluent and high-net-worth clients, featuring private meeting spaces and premium finishes. These centers, with 21 currently operating and 10 more planned by year-end 2026, aim to deepen relationships and unlock cross-selling opportunities across mortgages, auto loans, investment products, and credit cards. This premium model mirrors Apple's successful retail strategy, where physical stores serve as brand experience centers rather than mere transaction points. Beyond affluent markets, Chase is also expanding into low-to-moderate income (LMI) and rural communities with "Community Centers." These centers are designed for community gatherings, financial health workshops, and small business pop-ups, staffed by Community Managers who provide financial education and support. This dual-pronged approach allows JPMorgan to capture both high-value and emerging market segments, aiming for 75% of Americans to be within a reasonable drive of a branch and over 50% within each state. The bank also reported a 20% productivity increase by bankers since 2019, indicating improved, relevant interactions are taking place in-branch. Ultimately, this physical expansion is about customer acquisition and retention in a competitive landscape. While digital channels are efficient, physical branches provide a tangible point of contact that builds trust and loyalty, especially for significant life events like securing a mortgage or planning for retirement. JPMorgan's ability to arbitrage its terrestrial presence, much like digital players optimize SEO, allows it to increase leads in dense areas and drive productivity within branches by targeting high-value products. This comprehensive strategy, combining digital leadership with a strategic physical presence, aims to create a formidable competitive advantage. The branch expansion is poised to significantly impact customer acquisition and engagement by offering a blended experience that caters to diverse preferences. While 54% of bank customers primarily use mobile apps and 22% prefer online banking via PC, a substantial portion still values or occasionally utilizes physical branches. An ABA survey found that 9% of consumers still prefer visiting a branch, and critically, 63% of consumers desire one-on-one personal conversations with bank representatives. This highlights the enduring importance of the human touch, especially for complex financial needs. JPMorgan's strategy directly addresses this demand for personalized interaction. By opening new branches and renovating existing ones, the bank aims to increase its physical touchpoints, making it easier for customers to access in-person advice and services. The bank has already seen positive results, with more than 75% of customer balances held by regular branch visitors, indicating that these locations foster deeper, more engaged relationships. The addition of 1,100 new employees as part of this expansion further underscores the commitment to human-led service, moving closer to a goal of adding over 10,500 Consumer Bank team members by year-end. The segmented branch strategy is key to optimizing engagement. J.P. Morgan Financial Centers, for example, are designed to attract and retain high-net-worth clients who often require sophisticated wealth management and advisory services. These clients, who may prefer digital for routine tasks, still value the privacy and personal attention offered by a dedicated financial advisor in a premium setting. Similarly, Community Centers focus on building trust and providing financial literacy in underserved areas, offering workshops on budgeting, saving, and fraud prevention to both customers and non-customers alike. This community-centric approach can foster loyalty and bring new customers into the Chase ecosystem. Moreover, the physical presence acts as a powerful marketing channel. Approximately 25% of branded credit cards are sourced at the branch level, demonstrating the effectiveness of in-person interactions for product origination. By strategically placing branches in high-density urban hubs and fast-growing regions, JPMorgan can increase brand visibility and capture new business checking accounts for small business owners. This hybrid model ensures that whether a customer prefers digital convenience or in-person expertise, Chase can meet them where they are, ultimately driving higher customer satisfaction and deeper relationships that influence loyalty and the bottom line. The immediate impact of JPMorgan's aggressive expansion strategy is a significant increase in operational costs, as evidenced by the projected $105 billion expense guidance for 2026. This represents a $9 billion jump from 2025 and includes substantial investments not only in physical branches but also in AI-driven automation. While the market reacted negatively to this "expense shock," viewing it as a drag on short-term earnings, the bank frames these expenditures as crucial long-term investments designed to enhance efficiency and drive future profitability. The cost of opening new branches and renovating 1,700 locations is considerable, encompassing real estate, construction, technology upgrades, and staffing. However, JPMorgan's internal data suggests a relatively quick return on investment, with a 4-year break-even on new branch builds. This rapid payback period, coupled with the reported $160 billion in incremental deposits attributed to branch effectiveness, indicates that the physical network is a highly productive asset. The bank's ability to increase branch productivity from $120 million to $230 million in deposits per branch, significantly outperforming peers, underscores the efficiency of its branch strategy. From a profitability standpoint, the strategy aims to boost Net Interest Income (NII) and fee-based revenue. While the bank's 2026 NII guidance of $103 billion suggests a plateauing of interest income, the branch expansion is designed to drive future growth through increased deposit share and cross-selling of higher-margin products like mortgages, auto loans, and investment services. The Asset & Wealth Management (AWM) segment, which often benefits from in-person advisory services, was a standout performer in recent earnings, further validating the investment in high-touch client experiences. However, the strategy is not without risks. The $105 billion investment budget must yield immediate productivity gains and demonstrable returns to justify the expense. If these investments fail to translate into sustained revenue growth or operational efficiencies, the bank might face pressure to implement more aggressive cost-cutting measures. Furthermore, potential regulatory headwinds, such as a proposed 10% cap on credit card interest rates, could compress margins in the consumer division, making the need for diversified revenue streams and efficient operations even more critical. JPMorgan's robust $4.7 billion credit provision provides a buffer against potential credit losses, but a sustained recession would test its projected 3.4% net charge-off rate for credit cards. For investors, JPMorgan's branch expansion strategy presents a complex picture of short-term expense pressure versus long-term strategic positioning. The initial market reaction to the $105 billion expense guidance for 2026 highlights investor sensitivity to increased spending, especially when coupled with a projected plateauing of Net Interest Income. However, the bank's historical resilience and proactive investments suggest a fundamental belief in the long-term value of its diversified model. JPM is currently trading at $309.97, near its 52-week high of $337.25, reflecting underlying confidence despite recent expense concerns. The investment thesis hinges on JPMorgan's ability to execute its hybrid strategy effectively, leveraging both its digital leadership and expanded physical footprint to capture market share and deepen customer relationships. The bank's strong financial fundamentals, including a P/E ratio of 15.17 and a robust Return on Equity (ROE) of 15.9%, indicate a well-managed institution. Its dividend yield of 1.9% with a payout ratio of 28.2% also offers a compelling return for income-focused investors, demonstrating the bank's capacity to return capital even amidst heavy investment cycles. This strategy also has significant implications for the broader banking sector. JPMorgan's massive investment budget, nearly equal to the market capitalization of many mid-sized banks, underscores a widening "innovation gap." Smaller and regional banks may struggle to keep pace with the technological demands of modern banking and the cost of maintaining a competitive physical presence. This could lead to further consolidation in the industry, with larger players like JPMorgan continuing to absorb market share and talent, as seen with its acquisition of First Republic Bank assets. Conversely, the technology and AI sectors stand to benefit significantly from JPMorgan's commitment to spend billions on automation, highlighting the critical role of firms providing the infrastructure for the "bank of the future." Investors should closely monitor the realization of AI-related cost savings and the stability of consumer credit as the 2026 fiscal year progresses. While geopolitical warnings and regulatory threats add layers of uncertainty, JPMorgan's proactive positioning suggests a strategic move to solidify its market leadership and navigate a volatile financial landscape, making it a key bellwether for the industry. JPMorgan Chase's bold move to expand its physical branch network, even as it pours billions into AI and digital transformation, signals a clear vision for the future of banking: a powerful hybrid model. This isn't a retreat from digital, but rather a sophisticated integration of in-person expertise with cutting-edge technology. The bank is betting that true competitive advantage lies in offering customers seamless, personalized experiences across all channels, from mobile apps to concierge-style financial centers. This strategy, while costly in the short term, is designed to fortify JPMorgan's position as the dominant player in the U.S. financial landscape. By strategically expanding its reach into new markets and deepening relationships with high-value clients, the bank aims to drive sustainable revenue growth and enhance customer loyalty. For investors, the long-term narrative of market share gains and operational efficiencies, underpinned by a resilient "fortress" balance sheet, could outweigh the immediate "expense shock." title: Is It All One Big AI Trade? - J.P. Morgan

Explore how this theme may influence portfolio strategy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the buzzword everywhere you go: The Nasdaq 100 is up +15% year to date (YTD), hyperscalers are expected to spend +$750 billion on capex (and that estimate seems to rise each earnings season), and LLM companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have increased revenues at an unbelievable pace. (Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate reportedly rocketed from $9 billion to $47 billion in about six months.) All of this is happening after two years of +20% S&P 500 returns, amid geopolitical conflicts, tariffs, the worst energy shock in history1 and consumer confidence near historic lows2 – so it’s understandable that many investors feel uneasy. A lot of attention this year has gone to chips and memory. Companies like Sandisk, TSMC, and SK Hynix are up sharply, and the semis index is up +39% YTD as semi net income is becoming a more significant contributor to the S&P 500. This line chart shows next-twelve-month net income as a percentage of the S&P 500 from 2020 through 2026, under the title "Semi net income has accelerated" with the subtitle "Next-twelve-month net income as a % of S&P 500." The vertical axis ranges from 4% at the bottom to 20% at the top in increments of 2%, and the horizontal axis spans years from '20 through '26 with annual markers. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: FactSet. Finance L.P. Data as of July 23, 2026." The line begins at approximately 5.5% in early 2020, moves in a narrow range between roughly 5% and 6% through 2020 and 2021, rises slightly to a local peak near 6.2% in mid-2021, then declines to a trough of approximately 4.5% in mid-2022. From late 2022 onward the line rises steadily and continuously, climbing from about 5% in early 2023 through roughly 6.5% by mid-2023, continuing upward to approximately 8% by early 2024, reaching about 9.5% by late 2024, and accelerating further to around 13% by mid-2025. The line then rises more steeply through late 2025, reaching approximately 15.5% to 16% before a sharp upward spike brings it to approximately 18.5% by the end of the series in 2026. But performance hasn’t been confined to a small corner of the market. Across the full AI value chain, the theme has been working. An analysis conducted of five different AI baskets containing 148 companies spanning the AI ecosystem (data centers, chips, memory, cooling, hyperscalers, electrification, software, etc.) revealed the following results: In other words, AI is showing up as a distributed theme across the value chain. AI and the AI supply chain are important drivers, but they’re not the only thing working. The most obvious non-AI driver this year has been geopolitics: With the conflict in the Middle East, energy is the top-performing sector in the S&P 500 so far this year, supported by elevated energy prices. That is an idiosyncratic driver but could reverse. Beyond that, there are more sustainable themes contributing to performance. Near-shoring remains top of mind, and industrials is a leading sector – driven not only by AI narratives, but also by a broader shift toward domestic and regional investment. Certain subsectors within healthcare and financials have performed well, as have certain materials. As Q2 earnings season ramps up, we expect 10 of 11 sectors to post positive earnings growth (six of those in double digits). Ultimately, AI is likely to be a success story for the entire market. If someone said, “I’m worried the email trade is taking over the market,” it might sound strange – the same goes for mobile. Those technological advancements became inseparable from corporate productivity and profitability. Over time, AI will become inseparable from the broader market as well. We’re just not there yet. The AI story is real and will likely be an integral part of portfolios in the years to come. But diversification, and the inherent importance it has for achieving your long-term goals, is still critical. One encouraging development over the past year is that when semis were “risk-off” (defined as one-month rolling compounded daily returns that are less than -5%), other sectors in the S&P 500 weren’t necessarily risk-off too. From a portfolio construction standpoint, this is positive: On days when the semi trade hasn’t worked, other parts of the portfolio have, on average, held up better. This bar chart shows the percentage of days each sector is risk-off when semiconductors are risk-off, year-to-date, under the title "Semis selloff ≠ market selloff" with the subtitle "% of days sector is risk-off when Semiconductors are risk off, Year-to-Date." The vertical axis ranges from 0% to 100% in increments of 10%, and the horizontal axis lists seven categories from left to right: Consumer Discretionary, Industrials, Financials, Consumer Staples, Health Care, Utilities, and Energy. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Note: Risk-off is defined as whenever 1-month rolling compounded daily returns are less than -5%." Each bar is labeled with its value at the top, and the bars are arranged in descending order: Consumer Discretionary is 86%, Industrials is 59%, Financials is 55%, Consumer Staples is 45%, Health Care is 45%, Utilities is 41%, and Energy is 18%. Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Note: Risk-off is defined as whenever 1-month rolling compounded daily returns are less than -5%. There’s also more breadth: YTD, the average stock is up more than the market-cap-weighted index. And importantly, the market is also not tech-blind – that is, not all tech is being treated equally. After years of nearly perfect correlation between semis and software, the two assets have become much less correlated over the past year as markets reassess who wins in an AI world. Once Claude Cowork came out, it became increasingly clear that parts of traditional software could be challenged as AI capabilities improve. This line chart shows the software 1-year rolling correlation to semiconductors from 2018 through 2026, under the title "Post Claude Cowork, Software and Semi correlations have plunged" with the subtitle "Software 1-year rolling correlation to Semiconductors." The vertical axis ranges from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.1, and the horizontal axis spans years from '18 through '26 with annual markers. A source note at the bottom reads "Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 3, 2026." A vertical dashed reference line is positioned near the far right at 2026 and is annotated "Claude Cowork launch." The line begins at approximately 0.65 in early 2018, rises to a range of about 0.75 to 0.80 through 2018 and 2019 with a peak near 0.82, then moves lower before dropping to approximately 0.56 in early 2020. It then rises to about 0.90 across 2020 into early 2021, declines through 2021 to around 0.65 to 0.70, and then drops to approximately 0.45 in late 2021 into early 2022. The line then rises unevenly through 2022 and 2023 to roughly 0.85 in mid-2023, moves lower through 2024 to about 0.63, and rises again to approximately 0.80 in mid-to-late 2025. At the point of the "Claude Cowork launch" reference line at 2026, the line turns downward and falls from about 0.78 to approximately 0.29 by the end of the series. Sources: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of July 17, 2026. Another divergence emerging more recently is within the hyperscalers. Hyperscaler capex has been the engine of the AI trade for the past few years: Hyperscalers spend, the market rewards them for impressive growth and the broader AI universe benefits alongside them. But markets are increasingly wary of sustained high spend as these behemoths gradually draw down their cash flows. Alphabet’s earnings results are a clear example. Despite delivering impressive cloud revenue and a continued ballooning backlog, investors focused on the other side of the equation: Management again guided capex higher and reported its first negative quarter of free cash flow since its IPO. We’re seeing the market become more critical – and more discriminating – ­across hyperscalers as investors try to separate AI winners from losers. Long-term, the success (or failure) of the hyperscalers to generate an acceptable return on investment on their heavy capex investments will likely be correlated with the returns of the AI ecosystem. Ultimately, we think we’re only in the early innings of the AI tech cycle as AI has become much more useful in agentic form. Over time, AI’s reach will continue to grow and extend well beyond technology alone. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation. Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations. In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether. The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5. Analysts employed by brokerage firms have been and continue to be overly optimistic with their recommendations. Since the ratings issued by these analysts are more favorable than their research would support because of the vested interest of their employers, they mislead investors far more often than they guide. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements. In addition, the different Zacks Rank grades are applied proportionately to all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide current-year earnings estimates. In other words, this tool always maintains a balance among its five ranks. Another key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank is freshness. The ABR is not necessarily up-to-date when you look at it. But, since brokerage analysts keep revising their earnings estimates to account for a company's changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in indicating future price movements. In terms of earnings estimate revisions for JPMorgan Chase & Co., the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has increased 5.1% over the past month to $24.39. title: What Does JPMorgan's Latest Dividend Declaration Signify - Kavout | AI
content: JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) continues to demonstrate its financial resilience and dedication to rewarding shareholders, with the latest quarterly dividend declaration of $1.50 per share reinforcing a bullish outlook for the banking giant. This consistent capital return strategy, backed by a fortress balance sheet and diversified revenue streams, makes JPM a compelling consideration for income-focused investors and those seeking stability in the financial sector. JPMorgan Chase's Board of Directors recently declared a quarterly dividend of $1.50 per share on its common stock, announced on May 18, 2026. This dividend is scheduled to be paid on July 31, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on July 6, 2026. This declaration is not merely a routine announcement; it serves as a strong indicator of the bank's robust financial standing and its confidence in future earnings, especially following a period of strategic capital allocation. The $1.50 per share dividend maintains the level set in previous quarters, including the one paid on April 30, 2026, which had an ex-dividend date of April 6, 2026. This consistency is a hallmark of JPM's approach to shareholder returns, which has seen the dividend per share grow by 15.9% year-over-year in fiscal year 2025. Such a track record, with 14 consecutive years of dividend increases through various economic cycles, speaks volumes about the sustainability of its payout. For investors, a stable and growing dividend from a financial titan like JPMorgan Chase offers a tangible return on investment, particularly in an environment where income generation remains a priority. The current trailing twelve months (TTM) dividend payout for JPM stands at $6.00, translating to a dividend yield of 1.9% based on the current share price of $306.74. This yield, while slightly below the industry average of 2.3% as noted by some analysts, is underpinned by a conservative payout ratio of 29.2%, leaving ample room for future increases and reinvestment into the business. JPMorgan Chase's TTM dividend payout ratio of 29.2% is a critical metric that highlights the bank's prudent capital management and strong financial health. This ratio indicates that less than a third of the bank's earnings are distributed as dividends, leaving a substantial portion for reinvestment, debt reduction, or share repurchases. For a financial institution, a conservative payout ratio is particularly important as it provides a buffer against unexpected economic downturns and regulatory changes, ensuring the stability of future payouts. This conservative approach is further supported by JPM's robust earnings per share (EPS) of $21.12 for the trailing twelve months. With the $6.00 annualized dividend, the earnings comfortably cover the payout, reinforcing the sustainability of the dividend stream. In fact, Simply Wall St analysts project the dividend to remain well covered by earnings, with a forecast payout ratio of 28% in three years, even as EPS is expected to grow by 23% over the next three years. This forward-looking stability provides a strong foundation for income-seeking investors. Beyond the payout ratio, JPM's overall financial strength is evident in its substantial capital base. As of December 31, 2025, the firm reported $4.4 trillion in assets and $362 billion in stockholders' equity. Chairman and CEO Jamie Dimon has consistently emphasized the bank's "fortress balance sheet," which includes $291 billion in CET1 capital and $1.5 trillion in cash and marketable securities. This significant excess capital and robust liquidity enable the bank to not only sustain its dividend but also to navigate various market conditions, including the Federal Reserve's stress tests, which JPM has consistently cleared. JPMorgan Chase's capital allocation strategy extends beyond just dividends, encompassing significant share repurchase programs that further enhance shareholder value. On July 1, 2025, the firm's Board of Directors authorized a new common share repurchase program of $50 billion. This authorization, used at management's discretion, complements the dividend strategy by reducing the number of outstanding shares, thereby boosting EPS and potentially the stock price over time. The combination of a consistent dividend and an active share repurchase program signals a comprehensive approach to capital return. This dual strategy is particularly attractive to investors, as it offers both immediate income and potential capital appreciation. Jamie Dimon highlighted this, stating that the intended dividend increase and the new share repurchase program represent a "sustainable level of capital distribution" supported by strong financial performance. This commitment is crucial for maintaining investor confidence, especially given the firm's leadership position in investment banking, consumer banking, and asset management. Furthermore, JPM's strategic investments in its core businesses and expansion initiatives demonstrate a forward-looking approach to growth. The bank plans to open more than 500 new branches by 2027, with 150 already established in 2024, despite the rise of digital banking. This initiative, alongside its expansion of digital retail banking in Germany by early 2026 and across the European Union, aims to tailor its network to client needs and boost cross-selling. These growth drivers, coupled with a rebound in investment banking activity, are expected to underpin future earnings, providing a solid foundation for continued capital returns. JPMorgan Chase's current valuation metrics present a nuanced picture for investors, balancing its strong fundamentals with its recent stock performance. The stock is currently trading at $306.74, reflecting a modest gain of +0.12% today. Over the past year, JPM shares have traded within a 52-week range of $260.31 to $337.25, indicating that the stock is currently positioned towards the higher end of this range. From a valuation perspective, JPM's TTM Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio stands at 14.52. This is slightly below the industry average of 14.95x as noted by Zacks Investment Research in September 2025, suggesting that the stock might not be excessively overvalued compared to its peers. However, Simply Wall St noted in May 2026 that JPM's forward 12-month earnings multiple of 15.39x compared to the industry's 14.95x indicates a "stretched valuation." This discrepancy highlights the importance of considering both trailing and forward-looking metrics. Despite some concerns about valuation, analyst sentiment remains predominantly positive. Of 28 analysts covering JPM, 12 rate it a Buy, 14 a Hold, and only 2 a Sell. The average target price is $328.00, which implies a potential upside of approximately 7% from the current price. This consensus suggests that while the stock has performed well, there is still room for appreciation, driven by resilient credit quality, updated investor day guidance, and generally constructive views on large diversified banks. The firm's robust Return on Equity (ROE) of 16.3% and revenue growth of 3.3% (FY2025 YoY) further underscore its operational efficiency and ability to generate profits, making the current valuation potentially justifiable for long-term holders. While JPMorgan Chase presents a compelling investment case, particularly for dividend-focused investors, it is crucial to consider the inherent risks and future opportunities that could influence its performance. One significant opportunity lies in the rebound of its Investment Banking (IB) business. After a slowdown in global deal-making in early 2022 due to geopolitical tensions and inflation, JPM's total IB fees in the Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB) segment rose 36% year-over-year in 2024. The healthy IB pipeline and an active M&A market are expected to drive stronger growth once macroeconomic conditions stabilize, with Douglas Petno, co-CEO of CIB, projecting low-double-digit year-over-year growth in IB fees for Q3 2025. However, the bank faces potential headwinds related to interest rate policy and net interest income (NII). While management projected NII of $95.5 billion for 2025, up more than 3% year-over-year, lower rates are expected to hurt the metric in 2026 as the Federal Reserve navigates rate policy. JPM's balance sheet is highly asset-sensitive, meaning declining rates could compress NII. This is a common challenge for large banks, with peers like Bank of America and Citigroup also anticipating modest NII compression over the medium term. On the risk side, asset quality deterioration remains a watch point. While JPM recorded negative provisions in 2021, a substantial rise in provisions occurred in subsequent years due to a worsening macroeconomic outlook. Management projects the card net charge-off rate to be 3.6% for 2025. However, lower rates could support asset quality by easing debt-service burdens and improving borrower solvency. JPM's extensive suite of services, from consumer banking to wealth management, diversifies its revenue streams, strengthening its resilience against sector-specific downturns and providing a buffer against these risks. JPMorgan Chase's consistent dividend declarations, including the latest $1.50 per share payout on July 31, 2026, underscore its financial strength and commitment to shareholders. The bank's conservative payout ratio of 29.2% and robust capital position provide a solid foundation for sustainable income. While valuation requires careful consideration, JPM's strategic growth initiatives and diversified business model position it well to navigate future economic shifts and continue delivering value. title: ‘The demographic dividend of the last 40 years is ending’: J.P. Morgan says the world is running out of the two things that kept interest rates down - Fortune
content:
In 2025, the IMF reported that, across the globe, companies, households, and countries had amassed $251 trillion in debt. Looking toward the end of 2026, J.P. Morgan has warned that interest rates on such borrowings are set to spike, owing largely to dwindling populations and diminishing fiscal discipline.In a note yesterday, JPMorgan’s Joyce Chang and team unpacked the “six D’s” that will shape the global economy: Deficits, deregulation, de-carbonization, de-population, de-globalization, and de-dollarization.Of these factors, two in particular will put upward pressure on borrowing rates around the world: Deficits and de-population. Turning first to deficits, JPM’s research team wrote that “a global breakdown in fiscal discipline is occurring in all corners of the world, and fiscal dominance is eclipsing monetary policy. Global public debt has reached $100 trillion, reducing fiscal space, while elevated deficits are driving up interest rates.” Among economists, there is some debate as to the extent to which deficits drive interest rates. The theory is that an expanding national debt may spark fears that the government is less creditworthy, and the Federal Reserve would then increase the money supply to reduce the value of the debt, therefore creating inflation. Governments have leaned on fiscal stimulus (via increased spending or tax cuts) heavily during the Iran crisis, the IMF reported in its most recent World Economic Outlook update. These increases to deficits—or reductions in government revenue—have been without “well-identified offsets, with few signs of rebuilding fiscal space,” JPM wrote. “Fiscal space” refers to a government’s ability to increase spending or lower taxes without jeopardizing its financial stability. “In the U.S., a larger stock of debt and higher interest rates, along with no political will to achieve fiscal consolidation anytime soon, point to higher term premium,” JPM adds, referring to the return lenders expect for holding long-term bonds, demanding higher rates as a result. “The unsustainable U.S. fiscal deficit has not yet caused much damage to the U.S. economy, since the U.S. has much more fiscal space than other countries,” Chang’s team added. The U.S. remains the safest and strongest country in a time of geopolitical upheaval, the note adds, suggesting risk to the debt outlook will come from “any dramatic military, political, energy security, or economic setbacks that make the U.S. no longer the safest and strongest.” Advanced economies are also facing declining birth rates and aging populations. Simply put, these economies will have a smaller labor supply to pay for goods and services needed by an older, non-working population. Demand for pension and healthcare expenditures will rise in many countries, notes JPM, while demand for public investments—such as defense, renewable energy, and infrastructure—is also intensifying. “Without offsetting measures such as higher government revenues, other public spending cuts or changes in the interest rate-growth differential, these spending pressures imply a substantial increase in public debt across jurisdictions beyond 2031,” the research adds. Currently, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget’s Social Security Countdown—the point at which benefits will have to be cut—stands at seven years and 10 months, and “neither political party is expected to act” until that cliff is met, America’s largest bank continues. “Neither political party is expected to act until the Social Security cliff approaches in 2032,” the note from America’s largest bank continues. It adds that some ~$600bn in debt would need to be issued to address the shortfall, and potentially further spending cuts and higher taxes. “We also note the demographic challenges that will lower savings and highlight the risk that aging populations and longevity could drive down equilibrium returns, with even funded systems struggling,” the team adds. “The demographic dividend that characterized the last 40 years is ending, and we view de-population as an underappreciated risk that will reduce savings and contribute to higher interest rates.” Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. title: Is it all one big AI trade? - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content: We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Artificial intelligence is the buzzword everywhere you go: The NASDAQ 100 is up +15% year-to-date, hyperscalers are expected to spend +$750 billion on capex (and that estimate seems to rise each earnings season), and LLM companies, such as Anthropic and OpenAI, have increased revenues at an unbelievable pace (Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate reportedly rocketed from $9 billion to $47 billion in about six months). All of this is happening after two years of +20% S&P 500 returns, amid geopolitical conflicts, tariffs, the worst energy shock in history1 and consumer confidence near historic lows2—so it’s understandable that many investors feel uneasy. A lot of attention this year has gone to chips and memory. Companies like Sandisk, TSMC and SK Hynix are up sharply, and the semis index is up +39% year-to-date as their net income is becoming a more significant contributor to the S&P 500. But performance hasn’t been confined to a small corner of the market. Across the full AI value chain, the theme has been working. An analysis conducted of five different AI baskets containing 148 companies spanning the AI ecosystem (data centers, chips, memory, cooling, hyperscalers, electrification, software, etc.) revealed the following results: In other words, AI is showing up as a distributed theme across the value chain. AI and the AI supply chain are an important driver, but they’re not the only thing working. The most obvious non-AI driver this year has been geopolitics: With the conflict in the Middle East, energy is the top-performing sector in the S&P 500 so far this year, supported by elevated energy prices. That’s an idiosyncratic driver but could reverse. Beyond that, there are more sustainable themes contributing to performance. Nearshoring remains top of mind, and industrials is a leading sector—driven not only by AI narratives, but also by a broader shift toward domestic and regional investment. Certain sub-sectors within healthcare and financials have performed well, as have certain materials. As Q2 earnings season ramps up, we expect 10 of 11 sectors to post positive earnings growth (six of those in double digits). Ultimately, AI is likely to be a success story for the entire market. If someone said, “I’m worried the email trade is taking over the market,” it may sound strange—same for “mobile.” Those are technological advancements that became inseparable from corporate productivity and profitability. Over time, AI will become inseparable from the broader market as well. We’re just not there yet. The AI story is real and will likely be an integral part of portfolios in the years to come. But diversification, and the inherent importance it has for achieving your long-term goals, is still critical. One encouraging development over the past year is that when semiconductors were “risk-off” (defined as one-month rolling compounded daily returns that are less than -5%), other sectors in the S&P 500 weren’t necessarily risk-off too. From a portfolio construction standpoint, this is positive: On days when the semiconductor trade hasn’t worked, other parts of the portfolio have, on average, held up better. Another divergence emerging more recently is within the hyperscalers. Hyperscaler capex has been the engine of the AI trade for the last few years: Hyperscalers spend, the market rewards them for impressive growth, and the broader AI universe benefits alongside them. But markets are increasingly wary of sustained high spend as these behemoths gradually draw down their cashflows. Alphabet’s earnings results are a clear example. Despite delivering impressive cloud revenue and a continued ballooning backlog, investors focused on the other side of the equation: Management again guided capex higher and reported its first negative quarter of free cash flow since its initial public offering (IPO). We’re seeing the market become more critical—and more discriminating—across hyperscalers as investors try to separate AI winners from losers. Long-term, the success (or failure) of the hyperscalers to generate an acceptable return on investment on their heavy capex investments, will likely be correlated with the returns of the AI ecosystem. Ultimately, we think we’re only in the early innings of the AI tech cycle as AI has become much more useful in agentic form. Over time, AI’s reach will continue to grow and extend well beyond technology alone. title: IRS boss Frank Bisignano has been accused of corporate spying — here’s what his old employer JPMorgan thinks - New York Post
content: See more of our coverage in your search results. Frank Bisignano allegedly spied on colleagues and misused company funds during his stint at JPMorgan Chase more than a decade ago. Those, at least, were the most sensational accusations in a lengthy Wall Street Journal report this week on Donald Trump’s IRS chief, who spent years at the big bank in various senior positions including co-chief operating officer working directly under CEO Jamie Dimon. Given the gravity of the story, I called JPMorgan, which had previously called Bisignano “a trusted adviser for years who we have known for decades and who is distinguished for his grit and determination. We applaud his service to our country both at the Social Security Administration and the IRS.” I then spoke to a senior JPMorgan executive who has firsthand knowledge of these more-than-a-decade-old claims. He said the “bank looked into the allegations of spying and misuse of funds and found no evidence of wrongdoing.” A spokeswoman for the Journal said: “Our reporting is accurate, thoroughly vetted, and backed by multiple knowledgeable sources. We stand behind the story.” Full disclosure: On The Money is a column in the New York Post, which shares a corporate owner with the Wall Street Journal. Back in the day, your humble correspondent spent years at the Journal reporting on Wall Street. That’s how I got to know the players involved in this story – from Bisignano to Dimon to Wells Fargo CEO Charles Scharf, who figures prominently in it – and also the president himself when he was a real estate mogul and reality TV star. In other words, I have no horse in this race other than having to cover something, which if true is a pretty big story. Consider, Bisignano now runs both the Internal Revenue Service and the Social Security Administration, which the Journal rightly says “puts him atop of two government organizations that store vast reams of sensitive financial data about every taxpayer.” Bisignano was brought on to apply his Wall Street knowledge to streamline government and make it more efficient for taxpayers. All of which makes this part of the story all the more serious: “More than a decade ago, he was co-chief operating officer at JPMorgan Chase, another perch that gave him visibility and authority over every part of a massive financial institution. At the bank, people familiar with the matter said, he spied on fellow executives—using his authority over the security department and position to access sensitive information and internal communications without an apparent business justification.” One of those executives was Scharf, then Dimon’s consumer bank chief, the paper said. There were other alleged misdeeds cited in the piece, some of which seem like normal grousing about a guy who, if you know Bisignano, can be a little rough around the edges. That’s despite the fact that at least one of those allegations also involves something pretty serious: the alleged “use of company resources for his own benefit, including allegations Bisignano misused the corporate jet for personal purposes, people familiar with the matter said.” Again, using the corporate jet for personal reasons is the easiest way to get jammed up on Wall Street, which is why I was a little shocked to read that part of the story. Knowing what I know about Bisignano, my first reaction is that he’s probably too careful to do something that dumb that would put him at odds with a legendary control freak like Dimon. That allegation, according to the bank executive who asked not to be quoted by name, was investigated as well and JPM “found no evidence,” the executive said. Bisignano, through a lawyer, denied that charge as well as the spying allegation. I asked Scharf about the mess. He tells me that he and Bisignano are friends, and that he has heard rumblings about spying in the past. “All I know is what I’ve seen and I’ve never seen any spying,” he said. Scharf, who left JPM in 2012, said he and Bisignano spoke after the story ran and Bisignano denied the matter. In fact the two “joked” about it. One possible explanation of what went down came from another former colleague who explained Bisignano’s role at JPM this way: “Bisignano was in charge of compliance (as co-COO) ALL senior managers were told to work with compliance, the in-house police in charge of monitoring emails internally as well as externally making sure we all were complying with firm policy. It’s now known as tech/opps but back in the day, those functions were known as back office. Frank was given the job by Jamie and made something of it. They looked at everything we did.” Sign up to receive On The Money by Charlie Gasparino in your inbox every Thursday. By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy. Again, the Journal cited multiple sources; Bisignano through his attorney denied each allegation. And remember, all this happened more than a decade ago. Since leaving JPM in 2013, Bisignano has had a pretty remarkable career as CEO of payments processor First Data, and later with Fiserv after the two merged and just before he joined Team Trump as a change agent to reform two institutions known for their bureaucratic bloat. To address those issues he recently hired another JPMorgan executive, Vince LaPadula as his No. 2 at the IRS. Before his exit from the big bank, LaPadula tells me he sat down with Dimon and asked if he should work for Bisignano. “Jamie told me absolutely… he’s Mr. Fix It.” One other question I have is why am I reading all of this now? title: Former JP Morgan banker allegedly pushed to keep Epstein as client - upi.com
content: July 23 (UPI) -- Former JP Morgan Chase investment banking boss Jes Staley pushed the bank to keep Jeffrey Epstein as a client despite red flags surrounding the late sex offender, House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer, R-Ky., said Thursday. "It appears that within JPMorgan there were flags -- red flags -- about Epstein, but Mr. Staley is on record defending Epstein and encouraging JPMorgan to keep him as a client," Comer told CNBC outside Staley's closed-door testimony before the committee. "So we have a lot of questions about that." Staley was Epstein's private banker at JP Morgan and stayed friends with him for years. "If it weren't for banks and bankers like Jes Staley, then Jeffrey Epstein would not have been able to continue to commit these crimes against women," Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said in a press conference Thursday. "He would not have continued to do some of the things that he did. But it was because of these banks that he was able to do so." More than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein appear in the files released by the Department of Justice last year. Some include Staley describing their friendship as "profound" and calling Epstein "family." "We have email documentation that in 2010 he was requesting and interacting with Jeffrey Epstein to procure women that he had sexual encounters with, and when he was asked in [the committee hearing] what happened and to describe those encounters, he could not recall," Rep. A confidential IPO filing from the ChatGPT maker is reportedly expected within weeks. Shares of Oculis Holding (OCS) fell more than 23% during Friday afternoon trading after the company reported topline results from its Phase 3 DIAMOND-1 and DIAMOND-2 trials of OCS-01 eye drops in patients with diabetic macular edema (DME). Shares of Firefly Aerospace (FLY) rose over 1% in overnight trading heading into Friday, shrugging off a discounted stock offering as investors focused on a growing list of catalysts, including fresh NASA lunar contracts and a setback for rival Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket program. FLY stock fell nearly 14% on Thursday, logging its worst session in over six months, with shares on track to three straight weeks of gains. However, shares are looking to record a third consecutive month in the green. Late Thursday, Firefly priced its public offering at $48 per share, representing a 3% discount to the stock’s last closing price. The offering consists of 12 million shares in total, including 4 million newly issued shares from Firefly and 8 million shares being sold by existing stockholders. Additionally, the selling stockholders granted underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to 1.8 million additional shares at the public offering price, less underwriting discounts and commissions. Firefly said it plans to use proceeds from its portion of the offering for general corporate purposes, including supporting growth initiatives and recently awarded programs. Earlier this week, the company announced a $75 million subcontract from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory to support the agency's MoonFall mission, part of NASA's broader Moon Base initiative. Under the agreement, Firefly's Elytra spacecraft will transport four autonomous drones to the Moon's south pole, where they will survey terrain, explore permanently shadowed regions and help identify resources such as water ice that could support future human missions. The award expands Firefly's growing lunar portfolio, which already includes multiple Blue Ghost missions under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services program. The company recently completed key testing milestones for Blue Ghost Mission 2 and continues advancing Missions 3 and 4 while expanding spacecraft production capabilities. The contract was announced alongside NASA's first phase of its Moon Base initiative, which is expected to include 25 launches, 21 lunar landings and four metric tons of cargo delivered to the Moon. Firefly was selected to deploy the first drones to the lunar surface using its Elytra spacecraft, while Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 cargo lander to deliver future lunar rovers. Other awards went to Lunar Outpost and Astrolab for rover development. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has also outlined plans to invest over $20 billion over the next seven years in lunar infrastructure as part of the agency's Moon Base and Artemis programs, which aim to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon later this decade. However, retail traders are now betting that a setback at Blue Origin could create an opening for rival launch providers such as Firefly.  Late Thursday, Blue Origin confirmed that its New Glenn rocket experienced an "anomaly" during a hotfire test at Cape Canaveral. The rocket exploded in a massive fireball, while preparations were underway for its anticipated fourth mission, which was expected to deploy Amazon's Project Kuiper satellites. All personnel were accounted for and safe, Blue Origin said. The incident marks another challenge for New Glenn, which is already years behind schedule and remains central to Blue Origin's efforts to compete with SpaceX in commercial launch services, national security missions and NASA programs. The setback follows issues during New Glenn's third flight in April, when the rocket's upper stage failed to generate enough thrust to place an AST SpaceMobile satellite into its intended orbit. The satellite ultimately reentered Earth's atmosphere. Meanwhile, NASA said it would work with its partners on a thorough investigation and will assess any potential impacts to Artemis and other lunar initiatives. Any prolonged delays to New Glenn could create opportunities for competing providers such as Firefly. Setbacks at major space companies have also previously lifted sentiment toward rivals. For example, shares of Rocket Lab attracted investor interest during previous uncertainty around Blue Origin's launch programs, as traders looked for alternative ways to gain exposure to the commercial space sector. title: House lawmakers grill former JPMorgan executive Jes Staley over Epstein ties - CNBC
content:
House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer said Thursday that former JPMorgan Chase investment banking chief Jes Staley encouraged the bank to retain Jeffrey Epstein as a client despite internal red flags about the convicted sex offender. “It appears that within JPMorgan there were flags — red flags — about Epstein, but Mr. Staley is on record defending Epstein and encouraging JPMorgan to keep him as a client,” Comer, R-Ky., told CNBC outside Staley’s closed-door interview with the committee. “So we have a lot of questions about that.” Staley served as Epstein’s private banker during his more than three decades at JPMorgan and maintained a close personal relationship with him for years. “If it weren’t for banks and bankers like Jes Staley, then Jeffrey Epstein would not have been able to continue to commit these crimes against women,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., an oversight committee member, said at a news conference Thursday. “He would not have continued to do some of the things that he did. But it was because of these banks, that he was able to do so.” U.K. regulators cited more than 1,000 emails between the two men, including messages in which Staley described their friendship as “profound” and referred to Epstein as “family.” “We have email documentation that in 2010 he was requesting and interacting with Jeffrey Epstein to procure women that he had sexual encounters with, and when he was asked in [the committee hearing] what happened and to describe those encounters, he could not recall,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., another oversight committee member, said at the news conference Thursday. Staley later became CEO of Barclays but resigned in 2021 amid a dispute with British regulators over how he characterized his relationship with Epstein. He subsequently lost an appeal of a decision banning him from the U.K. financial industry for misleading regulators about those ties. JPMorgan agreed in 2023 to pay $290 million to settle a lawsuit brought by Epstein’s victims and $75 million to resolve a separate case brought by the U.S. Virgin Islands, without admitting liability. The bank later reached a confidential settlement with Staley. Democrats on the oversight committee said that JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon’s name did not come up during their questioning. title: Patchmageddon - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content: The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The race to patch software vulnerabilities before zero-day cyber-exploitations proliferate Highly capable frontier AI models can now detect previously unknown vulnerabilities in software and operational hardware at massive scale. As a result, state-grade cyber capabilities will become increasingly accessible to actors with malicious intent such as ransomware operators motivated by profit, terrorists or hacktivists with no goal but destruction. Unfortunately, it’s taking longer to patch vulnerabilities just as attacker time to exploit is falling; the average time between disclosure of a vulnerability and its first exploitation has now fallen to zero days. In May 2026, Anthropic reported that of 530 high and critical vulnerabilities reported to maintainers, only 75 had been patched. Even when patches exist, companies often don’t respond in time: in ~60% of breaches, a patch was already available at the time of compromise. I partnered with JP Morgan’s Cybersecurity Teams to get into the details on this critical national security issue. In “Patchmageddon” we review how cyber risks have changed, the underappreciated breadth and risks from open source code, the risks to physical infrastructure and some guidance what business owners, software developers and the Federal government should be doing to mitigate the potential consequences. MICHAEL CEMBALEST: All right. Good morning, everybody. This is the July Eye on the Market podcast. This one's called The Summer I Turned Pretty, which I'll explain. Cautious about zero-day cyber attacks resulting from the latest frontier AI models, and that's going to be the bulk of the discussion on today's podcast, and, also, cautious about some market technicals and some growing challenges to the frontier labs from both new open and closed weight models. And let's start with some of the market technical issues. And there's a bunch of people that have been writing similar things. This is some work a colleague in the investment bank, Jason Hunter, has done. If you look back to the late 1990s, there was a point at which the communications stocks flatlined, even though the infrastructure stocks kept on rising. And as a proxy for that, think about Juniper Networks and Verizon and things like that. So you had this period on the market where the front end, which was the communication services stocks, started to flatline, but the infrastructure stocks kept going, and it was a bit of a head fake to the market. We're having a little bit of a parallel right now because the hyperscalers, which are the front end of this AI boom, are seeing their stock prices stagnate and their free cash flow fall, even as the semiconductor and other infrastructure providers and optical networking companies are continuing to go up. So there are some parallels here that I think we need to think about because you always want the caboose going slower than the front of the engine, and that's not what's happening. There are also some serious challenges to the frontier labs-- and by that, I'm obviously referring to Anthropic and OpenAI-- coming from a whole bunch of new models. And for those of you consuming this in video form, you can see this really colorful chart that's become somewhat standard in discussions about these different models. On the y-axis, you have some kind of measure of their productivity and performance. In this case, it's a benchmark focused on math and reasoning and coding tasks from this group, Artificial Analysis. And the x-axis is typically in log scale. And importantly, it's not cost per token, it's cost per task, because models can differ on the intensity of how many tokens they use and need. So it's better to just look at net of that efficiency, what's the overall cost of a task. And this curve used to be such that OpenAI and Anthropic frontier models were way better than everything else. Now, you can slide to the left on this chart. And Meta has a new model. SpaceXAI has a new Grok model. There's a new Chinese model where, all of a sudden, you're looking at models whose performance isn't that different from the best OpenAI and Anthropic models at either a third or a tenth of the cost. And so, I can imagine there's a lot of CFOs-- and I've spoken to some of them already-- that are starting to think about, hey, maybe these models can work for us on certain tasks. Not all of them, but some of them are having a bit of a sticker shock on the token bills that they've been paying. So there's two pieces to the Eye on the Market that are coming out today. One of them is on the cyber issue, and the other one is on these market technical and frontier lab challenges. And all that information is in the email. Just two quick things-- Thinking Machines, which was launched by some people that used to work at OpenAI, finally released their model. And as expected, it looks pretty good. And it's a mixture of experts' model, and I wouldn't be surprised if they were a serious challenger as well. And you're probably hearing a lot about Kimi K3 from a company called Moonshot. It's Chinese. And just to give you a sense, it costs about 30% as much in terms of input and output tokens as some of the other best models with similar performance. So, again, take a look at the Eye on the Market today for that. OK, so today is a first. So I'm having a co-host on the podcast, which I haven't done before. I should probably do that more often because some of our listeners probably are tired of hearing me drone on and on. But Pat Opet is here, and Pat is the Global Chief Information Security Officer at JP Morgan. And you've been at JP Morgan for more than a decade? MICHAEL CEMBALEST: 12 years. And Pat and his various teams have worked and helped me write a piece called, "Patchmageddon, the race to patch software vulnerabilities before zero-day cyber exploitations proliferate." So a lot of jargon involved, but Pat's here to make sure that everybody understands in layman's terms as much as we can what's going on. Thank you. And welcome to the podcast. PAT OPET: Well, thanks for having me. I'm excited to be here. MICHAEL CEMBALEST: I know. I might do this again. So, even before Mythos came along, right-- because Mythos was a bit of a shock to the system earlier this year. Even before Mythos came along, the data that your team shared with me shows that the pace at which vulnerabilities in the systems that big companies use were being found and disclosed at a much faster rate than they're patched. MICHAEL CEMBALEST: And what's it like to be inside a large organization where it's raining vulnerabilities, and you have to patch them? PAT OPET: Look, it's very difficult. And obviously, a lot of automation and tooling has been built over many years to help find vulnerabilities in software. But there isn't so much automation and tooling that helps organizations fix vulnerabilities. Fixing vulnerabilities requires putting new software in production. That often means that you have to do thorough testing to ensure that the new software you're putting in production doesn't break any other features. And for companies like ours, where continuity of operation is very important for our customers, that's a very careful process. Multiply that by the various industries and the difficulty in, perhaps, reaching the software that has to be put in production. Think like industrial control systems that aren't easily accessible or teams that don't have sufficiently sized technical teams. It becomes really onerous to keep up with the rate by which vulnerabilities are being found. MICHAEL CEMBALEST: So analyses differ here, right? But this chart is a proxy for, how long does it take for organizations to remediate things that need to be fixed? That's the gold line. And then the falling blue line is Time To Exploit, right? MICHAEL CEMBALEST: TTE-- why is that such an important concept for people to understand? Because I've been seeing it everywhere. PAT OPET: Yeah, so when a vulnerability is found, it is a flaw in a piece of software that could be abused by an attacker. The exploitation process is the attacker actually abusing that software. And so, typically, if you look back several years, teams had time, days, between a vulnerability being discovered and an attacker weaponizing that vulnerability. But through, again, new tooling, and in particular, various AI systems, attackers can now exploit vulnerabilities much more quickly to the point where attackers are actually both discovering the vulnerabilities and exploiting the vulnerabilities before the defenders even know they exist. That is colloquially called a zero-day, which is now dominating the headlines. MICHAEL CEMBALEST: Yes, and in this chart, in 2020, there was 30 days in between the disclosure of eligibility and its first exploitation. And those numbers have fallen basically to zero. And obviously, what industries are at risk? A lot of them and across a lot of different parts of the economy. And so it's not like one particular industry is more at risk than others. The ECB put out this financial stability review, and I thought it was kind of spooky that the largest component of who's doing this fell into a category called unknown. Why is it so hard to know who's doing it? Is it just the nature of-- PAT OPET: Just, what's called attribution in cybersecurity, associating an activity with an attacker depends on tradecraft and tooling and patterns. And over time, state actors or criminal actors have either diversified their supply chain, so it's not just them or their team doing an action, and they depend on many different parts of the community.
